system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 12 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2144-06-28 10:30:00 to 2144-07-09 15:44:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted with malaise, fever, and concerns for urinary tract infection and left hip ulcer infection. He has a complex history including paraplegia, chronic indwelling Foley catheter, recurrent UTIs, and chronic kidney disease. The catheter balloon was found to be malpositioned, causing frequent dislodgement and contamination. Urine cultures repeatedly showed mixed flora, indicating contamination rather than true infection, so antibiotics were withheld per infectious disease recommendation to avoid resistance. CT imaging showed no evidence of pyelonephritis or osteomyelitis, though chronic hip changes and synovitis were noted. His creatinine increased slightly, attributed to hypovolemia, and improved with IV fluids. The left hip ulcer was assessed by plastics and deemed non-infected. On the morning of discharge, the patient reported coughing up blood, but evaluation revealed no active bleeding, likely due to brown soda discoloration. He was discharged home with plans for urinary diversion surgery, follow-up with urology and plastics, and instructions to seek care if bleeding recurred.

Mr. ___ was admitted to the Urology service after undergoing 
ileal conduit urinary diversion.  No concerning intraoperative

Throughout the post-operative course, the patient was

regularly refused left trochanteric wound exams, dressing 
changes, vital signs, physical therapy, and transferring out of 
bed to chair. 

Patient received ___ intravenous antibiotic 
prophylaxis and deep vein thrombosis prophylaxis with 
subcutaneous heparin. Post-operatively, he had an NGT to low 
wall suction and PCA for pain control. A PICC line was placed 
POD1 due to poor venous access after discussion with nephrology. 
 Labs were checked and electrolytes repleted.  Chronic pain was

uncooperative with medical, nursing, and ancillary staff. He 
regularly refused left trochanteric wound exams, dressing 
changes, vital signs, physical therapy, and transferring out of 
bed to chair. 

Patient received ___ intravenous antibiotic 
prophylaxis and deep vein thrombosis prophylaxis with 
subcutaneous heparin. Post-operatively, he had an NGT to low 
wall suction and PCA for pain control. A PICC line was placed 
POD1 due to poor venous access after discussion with nephrology. 
 Labs were checked and electrolytes repleted.  Chronic pain was 
consulted for assistance given his long pain history. The wound 
care / ostomy nurse was consulted for ostomy teaching and left 
trochanteric dressing changes.  Per their recommendations, 
Plastic Surgery was consulted for bedside debridement. On POD2, 
the patient's NGT was removed after clamp trial demonstrated 
minimal residual. On POD4, the patient was febrile to 102.5. CT 
scan demonstrated non-specific post-surgical changes.  Cultures 
were sent and infectious disease was consulted.  Due to his 
history of resistant past infections. He was started on 
meropenem on POD5 for which he completed 7 days.

The rest of his post-operative course was essentially 
unremarkable. On POD5, he was able to self-disimpact.  His diet 
was gradually advanced and the patient was transitioned from IV 
pain medication to his home oral pain medication with chronic 
pain service input.  The ostomy nurse saw the patient for ostomy 
teaching.  At the time of discharge the surgical wound was 
healing well with no evidence of erythema, swelling, or purulent 
drainage.  The ostomy remained perfused and patent and the 
ureteral stents were visible.  On day of discharge, POD11, the 
ureteral stents were removed.  The surgical staples were removed 
and replaced with Steri-Strips.  His PICC line was discontinued 
after completing a final dose of IV antibiotics.  Post-operative 
follow up appointments were arranged/discussed and the patient 
was discharged home with visiting nurse services to further 
assist the transition to home with ostomy care and physical 
therapy. His PICC line and ureteral stents were removed before 
discharge and he was offered bactrim antibiotic, to start prior 
to discharge so that he may be observed (he refused). He was 
discharged home with ___ and escorted by his mother and 
god-daughter.

STUDY:  Portable abdomen, ___.

CLINICAL HISTORY:  ___ man with ileal conduit and bilateral ureteral
stent placement.

FINDINGS:  Comparison is made to previous study from ___.

Bilateral ureteral stents are seen.  The right-sided stent appears low. 
Additional stents are seen extending out to the ileal conduit in the right
lower abdomen.  There is diastasis of the pubic symphysis.  There is chronic
dislocation of the left hip.  Lower spinal hardware is seen.  Severe
degenerative changes of the right hip are seen.  No free intra-abdominal gas
is present.

STUDY:  AP chest; ___.

CLINICAL HISTORY:  ___ man with  PIC line placement.

FINDINGS:  Comparison is made to previous study from ___.

There is a right-sided PIC line, the distal tip is in the mid right atrium. 
This could be pulled back 4 cm for more optimal placement.  There are no
pneumothoraces.  There are low lung volumes with some atelectasis at the lung
bases.  Spinal hardware is seen.

EXAMINATION:  CHEST (PORTABLE AP)

INDICATION:  ___ year old man s/p ileal conduit urinary diversion  // Post
opertive fever, rule out pneumonia

TECHNIQUE:  Portable chest radiograph

COMPARISON:  ___

FINDINGS: 

Right PICC terminates in the mid to lower SVC.  Lung volumes remain low and a
linear atelectasis in the left mid lung field is unchanged. No pleural
effusion, pneumothorax, or new parenchymal opacity. Spinal hardware is again
partially imaged.

IMPRESSION: 

Low lung volumes. No evidence of pneumonia.

EXAMINATION:  CT ABD AND PELVIS W/O CONTRAST

INDICATION:  ___ year old man w/ fever s/p ileal conduit urinary diversion  //
please image abdomen and pelvis to rule out intraabdominal abscess,
osteomyelitis of hip

TECHNIQUE:  Axial CT images of the abdomen and pelvis were obtained without
intravenous related to patient's renal failure. Sagittal and coronal reformats
were prepared.

DLP:  542 mGy-cm

COMPARISON:  Prior CT scan from ___.

FINDINGS: 

ABDOMEN:

Previously identified tiny 5 mm left lower lobe subpleural nodule (2:7)
remains unchanged. There is evidence of bibasilar atelectasis.

Beam hardening artifact from spinal hardware somewhat limits assessment of the
abdomen and pelvis. Liver demonstrates normal attenuation. Within the
limitations of an unenhanced CT, no focal hepatic lesions. To the extent
assessed, the gallbladder, spleen, adrenal glands and pancreas are
unremarkable. A tiny accessory spleen is identified. The kidneys are atrophic.
Since the prior study, the patient is status post-cystectomy with a ileal
conduit. Bilateral ureteric stents are identified. Soft tissue thickening
surrounds the left ureteric stent, a nonspecific (04:25). No ascites. No
retroperitoneal or intraperitoneal lymphadenopathy. The stomach is
unremarkable. Slightly distended loops of small bowel are identified diffusely
(02:25), measuring up to 3.5 cm, with no definite transition point, likely
related to ileus.

PELVIS:

Rectum and sigmoid colon is unremarkable. Trace pelvic free fluid is
identified. Slightly enlarged bilateral inguinal lymph nodes are identified
(2:95, 85, 90), measuring up to 1.5 cm, likely reactive. Slightly prominent
external iliac chain lymph nodes are also identified bilaterally. Multiple
surgical clips are identified in the pelvis. Fat stranding is identified
within the pelvis, likely related to the recent surgery. A pelvic drain is
identified entering while left anterior pelvic wall. A tiny locule of air is
identified at the lower anterior pelvis, likely postsurgical.

OSSEOUS STRUCTURES:

Dysmorphic bony pelvis is again noted. Superior and posterior dislocation of
left femoral head relative to the acetabulum remains unchanged. Well
corticated fragments of left acetabulum remain unchanged. A skin defect
lateral to the left greater trochanter is again visualized. No definite
increase in soft tissue density of the subcutaneous tissues at this level. No
subcutaneous locules of air are identified. Focal area of lucency in the
proximal femur (2:85), remains unchanged. A skin defect is again identified
posterior to the left acetabulum (2:86), and remains unchanged compared to
prior study. Heterotopic bone formation adjacent to right greater trochanter
remains unchanged. A well-corticated lucency at the right femoral neck (2:93),
remains unchanged. Generalized fluid and soft tissue surrounding the hip
joints bilaterally also does not demonstrate significant change compared to
prior study.

Patient is status post laminectomy and posterior fusion from T9 through L2
with pedicle screws of L1 and L2. No evidence of hardware complication. T12
compression deformity remains unchanged. Left iliac wing donor site is again
noted.

IMPRESSION:


1. Status post ileal conduit urinary diversion. Bilateral ureteric stents
identified. Atrophic native kidneys.  Nonspecific soft tissue thickening
surrounds the left ureteric stent, likely related to inflammatory change.
2. No loculated fluid collections identified in the abdomen or pelvis to
suggest abscess formation.
3. Dysmorphic bony pelvis as seen previously, with postero-superior
dislocation of left femoral head. Skin defects identified lateral to left
greater trochanter and posterior to left acetabulum are unchanged. Generalized
fluid and soft tissues surrounding both hip joints does not demonstrate any
significant change compared to prior study. No new areas of lucency or
sclerosis to suggest osteomyelitis, however osteomyelitis is not excluded. If
there is persistent clinical concern regarding osteomyelitis, a nuclear
medicine white blood cell scan or gallium scan could be performed.
4. Generalized fluid and soft tissue surrounding the hip joints bilaterally
does not demonstrate significant change compared to prior study.
5. Stable 5 mm left lower lobe subpleural nodule.
6. Distended loops of small bowel, with no definite transition point, likely
related to ileus.
7. Enlarged bilateral inguinal lymph nodes and prominent external iliac chain
lymph nodes, presumably reactive.
8. Fat stranding within the pelvis, and a tiny locule of air in the lower
anterior pelvis, likely postsurgical.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. ___. I’m Dr. ___, your urologist. You’re here today for your ileal conduit surgery. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m okay, just nervous. This is a big surgery, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It is, but it’s also very necessary. Your incontinence has been causing serious skin breakdown, and this surgery should help stop that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, the sores on my hip won’t heal. I just want this fixed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll take care of it. The plan is to create a new way for urine to leave your body using a piece of your intestine. You’ll have a stoma on your belly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no more catheter down there?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. The catheter has been causing leakage and irritation. This new system should stop that completely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you. When do we start?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be taken to the OR shortly. We’ll see you when you wake up in recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You made it through surgery fine. You now have an ileal conduit. There are stents in place to help the connections heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How’s the stoma looking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Pink, moist, and draining well—perfect. You also have a PICC line now because your veins were hard to access. It’ll help with antibiotics and fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t like needles. Can’t I just take pills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. Your kidney function is reduced, and we need to make sure the antibiotics work. The PICC line helps us give them safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are improving. Hemoglobin was low yesterday, but it’s coming up. We’re watching your creatinine closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My stomach feels bloated. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your bowels are still waking up after surgery. You have an NG tube to help with that. We’ll remove it once things start moving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—your NG tube came out this morning. You passed the clamp trial, so no more suction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I eat now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with clear liquids and see how you do. If no nausea, we’ll advance your diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a fever last night—102.5. We’re checking cultures and getting a CT to make sure there’s no infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is something wrong with the surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT showed normal post-op changes—no abscess or pneumonia. But your urine culture grew E. coli, so we’re starting antibiotics as a precaution.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: E. coli again? I’ve had that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and because of your history of resistant infections, we’re using meropenem. It’s strong but safe for your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count is coming down. That’s a good sign the antibiotics are working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still feel tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Recovery takes time. Your body’s healing. We’ll keep helping with pain and nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT confirmed no abscess or osteomyelitis. Your fever is likely from the surgical site reacting, not a deep infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my hip sore? No one’s looked at it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve asked wound care and plastics to help. They recommend a bedside debridement to help it heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing better. Your diet’s advanced to soft foods, and you’re managing pain with oral meds now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I took my oxycodone this morning. It helped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. The chronic pain team adjusted your plan so you’re not on the IV PCA anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count is down to 17.9, and creatinine is stable. You’re healing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. You still need IV antibiotics for a few more days. But we’re getting close.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest urine culture showed yeast. It’s common after antibiotics. We don’t need to treat it unless you have symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, not at all. Just something we monitor. Your blood cultures were negative, so no bloodstream infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Almost there. One more dose of IV antibiotics tomorrow. Your stoma is healthy, and the wound is clean.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been practicing with the ostomy bag. It’s weird, but I think I can manage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. The nurse will keep teaching you, and you’ll have visiting nurses at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. We’ll remove the stents and your PICC line. Then you can go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Both today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The stents have done their job. We’ll take them out at the bedside. The PICC comes out after your last antibiotic dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stents are out. You did great. No pain, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Felt a little pressure, but okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: PICC line is out. The site’s covered, and you can shower in a couple days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What meds do I take at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll restart most of your home meds. We’re adding Bactrim for seven days to prevent infection and Vesicare to help with bladder spasms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to Bactrim.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see that. We discussed it. The benefit outweighs the risk, and we’ll watch you closely. But you refused to start it here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll take it at home if I have to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Just call us if you develop a rash or fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your staples are out, replaced with Steri-Strips. Keep the area dry for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the hip sore?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not infected, but it’s slow to heal. Plastics will see you as an outpatient. Keep using the special dressing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. Your mom and goddaughter are here. Visiting nurses will help with your stoma and therapy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well. Remember: no heavy lifting, keep the incision dry, and call us if you have fever, redness, or pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Urology in two weeks. Plastics and primary care will also see you. Take care, Mr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The stents and PICC line are fully removed. You’re officially discharged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. Keep up the good work with your care team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take these discharge instructions and the ostomy guide. Call us with any concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll read them tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Safe travels. We’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will wheel you out now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, let’s go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Remember to follow up with all your specialists.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t miss them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call us if you have any issues with the stoma or pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Get some rest at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll talk soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Bye for now.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted for ileal conduit urinary diversion due to severe urinary incontinence causing recurrent skin breakdown and stage IV pressure ulcers. The surgery was performed successfully, and he recovered without intraoperative complications. Post-operatively, he developed a fever on POD4, prompting a CT scan that showed nonspecific post-surgical changes without abscess or pneumonia. Urine culture grew E. coli, leading to a seven-day course of meropenem. His white count improved, and he transitioned from IV to oral pain medication. The NG tube was removed on POD2, diet advanced, and ostomy care was taught. On POD11, ureteral stents and the PICC line were removed, staples were replaced with Steri-Strips, and he was discharged home with visiting nurse services. He refused Bactrim initiation in the hospital but agreed to take it at home. Follow-up was arranged with urology, plastics, and primary care.
